analysis.body:
According to the Census Bureau's Business Time Use Survey, artificial intelligence adoption in construction stands at 16.0% of firms, up from 14.3% in the prior period. This represents the most direct measurement available of AI use across the sector, based on whether businesses reported using AI in the preceding two weeks.

The construction industry's AI deployment centers on applications that address persistent operational challenges. BuiltWorlds, which runs sector intelligence through member networks and annual conferences, identifies AI and machine learning use cases spanning the entire architecture, engineering, and construction workflow, from preconstruction planning through building operations and systems management. The sector intelligence community emphasizes data centers and AI infrastructure as emerging focus areas within the broader buildings innovation landscape, alongside examination of how solutions are being implemented at both project and enterprise levels.

The capital ecosystem tracking construction technology adoption includes both specialized contech investors and the broader proptech movement. CREtech, which hosts the industry's largest real estate AI conference, reports that major construction firms, developers, and investors are actively deploying AI across their portfolios, with sessions led by operators at the CIO, CEO, and managing director level. This indicates that adoption is concentrated among larger, capital-intensive market participants with resources to implement and integrate new technologies.

The trade association perspective comes from the Associated General Contractors of America, which surveys technology adoption across its membership of over 27,000 firms. AGC's research priorities center on construction input costs, labor availability, and workforce challenges, reflecting the sector's ongoing struggle to fill openings despite softer market conditions. While AGC tracks adoption broadly, the excerpts provided do not detail specific AI deployment patterns or vendor concentration.

For construction firms considering AI deployment, the material suggests that adoption remains concentrated among larger operators and that real-world case studies and peer implementation strategies are driving decision-making. The sector's intelligence networks emphasize lessons learned from active deployments rather than theoretical frameworks, indicating that evidence of ROI and operational fit, rather than vendor hype, guides procurement choices among contractors.

https://cretech.com/.brief: According to the page, CREtech New York 2026 will be held at the Javits Center in New York City on October 20, 21, 2026, and will bring together 3,000 leaders, 150 speakers, and more than 20,000 pre-scheduled 1:1 meetings. The event is described as a leading real-estate AI conference where sessions are led by operators actively deploying AI in their portfolios, offering real strategy rather than theory. The conference aims to connect owners, developers, investors, occupiers, construction firms, brokers, and tech leaders to discuss AI’s impact on real-estate assets. Tickets are limited, and sponsors and partners are said to represent companies shaping the future of real-estate in the age of AI.

https://builtworlds.com/.brief: BuiltWorlds operates a membership network for buildings and infrastructure professionals. The organization hosts an annual Buildings Conference addressing innovation in building development, design, materials and systems, with particular focus on data centers and AI infrastructure. It also runs an annual AI/ML Conference exploring artificial intelligence and machine learning adoption across the architecture, engineering, construction and operations industry, covering implementation strategies, use cases, and lessons learned from companies deploying these technologies.
